overview: In Go, errors are ordinary values. There is no exception mechanism for normal failures; instead a function returns an `error` alongside its result, and the caller inspects it explicitly.

The `error` type is a tiny built-in interface with a single method, `Error() string`. Anything that implements that method is an error, which makes errors composable, comparable, and testable like any other value.

The dominant idiom is the `(result, error)` return signature checked with `if err != nil { return err }`. Combined with `errors.New`, `fmt.Errorf` with the `%w` verb, sentinel errors, and custom error types, this gives Go a precise, explicit error-handling model.
learningObjectives: Explain the built-in `error` interface and why 'errors are values' is central to Go.
Create errors with `errors.New` and `fmt.Errorf`, and add context by wrapping with `%w`.
Inspect error chains using `errors.Is` (sentinel match) and `errors.As` (extract a concrete type), and define your own `ErrXxx` sentinels and `XxxError` types.
Recognize when to wrap versus annotate, contrast errors with panic/recover, and avoid the typed-nil-in-interface pitfall.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: `error` is a predeclared interface type defined as `type error interface { Error() string }`. An error value is any value whose dynamic type implements that single method; functions communicate failure by returning a non-nil error as their last return value.
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Instead of throwing an exception, a Go function hands you back two things: the answer and a possible problem. If the problem (`err`) is not nil, something went wrong and you decide what to do. An error is just a value that knows how to describe itself as a string.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Go was released in 2009 with errors-as-values from the start, a deliberate reaction to the hidden control flow and overhead of try/catch exceptions in C++/Java. For years developers hand-wrote context strings with `fmt.Errorf`. Go 1.13 (2019) standardized error chains by adding the `%w` wrapping verb plus `errors.Is`, `errors.As`, and `errors.Unwrap` in the standard library, formalizing patterns the community had built in packages like `github.com/pkg/errors`.

whyItMatters.business: Explicit errors make failure modes visible in code review and in production logs, so teams diagnose customer-facing incidents faster and ship features with fewer silent data-corruption bugs.
whyItMatters.engineering: Treating errors as values means they can be returned, stored, compared, wrapped, and unit-tested with ordinary tooling, eliminating an entire category of invisible control flow.
whyItMatters.scalability: Servers handling millions of requests need predictable failure handling; a non-nil check on the hot path is essentially free compared to stack-unwinding exceptions.
whyItMatters.cost: Catching and classifying errors precisely (retryable vs fatal) prevents wasteful retries and runaway resource use, directly reducing compute and on-call cost.
whyItMatters.reliability: Forcing the caller to acknowledge every error at the call site is why well-written Go services degrade gracefully instead of crashing on the first unhandled condition.

coreComponents.name: error interface
coreComponents.definition: The predeclared `interface { Error() string }` that all errors satisfy.
coreComponents.purpose: Provide a single, uniform type for representing failures.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Expose a human-readable message via Error(); act as the common return type for failing operations.

coreComponents.name: errors package
coreComponents.definition: Standard library package with New, Is, As, Unwrap, and Join.
coreComponents.purpose: Create errors and inspect error chains without fragile string matching.
coreComponents.responsibilities: errors.New makes a basic error; errors.Is/As walk the wrapped chain; errors.Unwrap peels one layer.

coreComponents.name: fmt.Errorf with %w
coreComponents.definition: Formatting helper that builds an error, optionally wrapping another with the %w verb.
coreComponents.purpose: Add contextual detail while preserving the underlying error for later inspection.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Produce a wrapping error whose Unwrap() returns the wrapped error.

coreComponents.name: Sentinel errors
coreComponents.definition: Exported package-level error variables compared by identity, e.g. io.EOF, sql.ErrNoRows.
coreComponents.purpose: Signal a specific, expected condition that callers branch on.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Be a stable, comparable value matched with errors.Is.

coreComponents.name: Custom error types
coreComponents.definition: Concrete structs implementing Error() string, often named XxxError.
coreComponents.purpose: Carry structured data (codes, fields) beyond a flat message.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Implement Error(); be extractable with errors.As; optionally implement Unwrap().

internalWorking: An interface value such as `error` is internally a two-word pair: a type descriptor (the dynamic type) and a data pointer (the value). `err != nil` is true whenever the type descriptor is non-nil, even if the data pointer is nil — the root of the typed-nil pitfall.

`errors.New(s)` allocates a small `*errorString` struct holding the string; its Error() returns that string. Two separate New calls with the same text are distinct, non-equal values, which is why sentinels must be shared package-level variables.
`fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err)` returns a `*fmt.wrapError` that stores the formatted message and the wrapped error, and exposes `Unwrap() error` returning the wrapped one, forming a linked chain.
`errors.Is(err, target)` walks the chain by repeatedly calling Unwrap, returning true if any link equals target (or implements `Is(error) bool` returning true).
`errors.As(err, &target)` walks the same chain and, at the first link assignable to *target's type, copies it into target and returns true, letting you recover structured fields.
`errors.Join(errs...)` (Go 1.20+) returns a single error whose Unwrap() returns `[]error`, so Is/As traverse multiple branches; printing it lists each on its own line.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: operation fails --> construct base error (errors.New / custom type) --> caller wraps with context (fmt.Errorf %w) --> error propagates up the call stack as a chain --> top-level handler inspects with errors.Is/As --> decide: log, retry, translate to HTTP status, or surface to user
dataFlowWalkthrough: A low-level function (e.g. a DB query) returns a sentinel like `sql.ErrNoRows` or a custom typed error.
Each intermediate caller adds context by returning `fmt.Errorf("doing X: %w", err)`, building a chain newest-on-top.
The error travels up through plain `if err != nil { return err }` checks without being inspected at every layer.
At a decision boundary (HTTP handler, CLI main), the code calls `errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows)` to map to a 404, or `errors.As(err, &ve)` to read a ValidationError's field.
Unmatched errors fall through to a generic 500/log path, with the full wrapped message (via `%v` or `%+v`) preserving the whole context chain for debugging.

keyTerminology.meaning: Built-in `interface { Error() string }` satisfied by all error values.
keyTerminology.importance: Defines what 'an error' is in Go; everything else builds on it.

keyTerminology.meaning: A package-level error variable (ErrXxx) compared by identity to signal a known condition.
keyTerminology.importance: Lets callers branch on specific outcomes like io.EOF without parsing strings.

keyTerminology.meaning: Embedding an underlying error inside a new one so the chain can be unwrapped later.
keyTerminology.importance: Adds context while keeping the original error inspectable with Is/As.

keyTerminology.meaning: Reports whether any error in the chain matches a target value.
keyTerminology.importance: The correct, refactor-safe replacement for `err == ErrFoo` once wrapping is involved.

keyTerminology.meaning: Finds the first error in the chain assignable to a target type and assigns it.
keyTerminology.importance: How you recover structured data from a wrapped custom error type.

keyTerminology.meaning: A nil pointer stored in an interface, making the interface non-nil.
keyTerminology.importance: A classic footgun: returning a nil `*MyError` as `error` yields `err != nil`.

importantConcepts.explanation: Because an error is just a value implementing an interface, you can compare it, store it in a slice, pass it to functions, wrap it, and test it — there is no separate exception type system or stack-unwinding machinery.

Use `%w` (wrap) when callers upstream might legitimately need to detect the underlying error with Is/As. Use `%v` (annotate) when the underlying error is an implementation detail you do not want to expose as part of your API contract.

Return errors for expected, recoverable conditions (bad input, missing file). Reserve panic for truly unrecoverable programmer bugs (impossible state, nil map write); recover only at well-defined boundaries like a server's per-request handler.

variationsAndTypes: Basic errors created with errors.New for simple, message-only failures.
Formatted/contextual errors built with fmt.Errorf, wrapping with %w or annotating with %v.
Sentinel errors (ErrXxx package variables) for known, branchable conditions like io.EOF and sql.ErrNoRows.
Custom error types (XxxError structs) carrying structured fields and optionally implementing Unwrap() and Is().
Aggregate errors via errors.Join, collecting multiple failures (e.g. validating many fields) into one inspectable value.
advantages: Explicit and visible: every failure must be acknowledged at the call site, no hidden control flow.
Composable: errors can be wrapped into chains that preserve context while staying machine-inspectable.
Cheap and predictable: a nil check costs nothing close to exception unwinding, ideal for hot paths.
Testable: because errors are values, you assert on them directly with errors.Is/As in unit tests.
Refactor-safe matching: errors.Is/As survive wrapping, unlike fragile string comparison or `==`.
disadvantages: Verbose: the `if err != nil { return err }` pattern repeats and can obscure the happy path.
Easy to lose context if you return the bare error without wrapping, making root-cause analysis harder.
Discipline-dependent: nothing forces you to wrap meaningfully or to check the right sentinel, so quality varies.
Subtle pitfalls like typed-nil-in-interface can cause errors that 'shouldn't exist' to be non-nil.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use the error-value model for all expected, recoverable failures — I/O, validation, network, parsing, business-rule violations — anywhere the caller can reasonably decide what to do next.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid using errors (and reach for panic) only for programmer mistakes that indicate a bug and cannot be sensibly handled at runtime, and avoid over-wrapping where it adds noise without new information.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Errors-as-values are like a delivery slip attached to a package. Instead of the courier shouting and abandoning the route (an exception), they hand you the box plus a slip: empty slip means success, a filled slip describes what went wrong. Each handler along the way can staple their own note on top (wrapping) without removing the originals, so when the package finally reaches you, the full chain of notes tells you exactly where and why it failed.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Go has no error handling because it lacks exceptions.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Go has rigorous error handling; it just models errors as return values instead of thrown exceptions, which is arguably more explicit.

commonMisconceptions.myth: panic/recover is Go's try/catch and should be used for normal errors.
commonMisconceptions.reality: panic is for unrecoverable bugs; using it for ordinary failures is non-idiomatic and brittle. Return an error instead.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You should always compare with `err == ErrFoo`.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Once errors are wrapped, `==` fails to match the chain. Use errors.Is(err, ErrFoo), which unwraps.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Returning a nil pointer as an error means err == nil.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A typed nil stored in the error interface is non-nil; the interface carries a type descriptor, so the nil check passes unexpectedly.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Classify errors (retryable, fatal, client-fault) so high-throughput services can shed or retry intelligently rather than treating every failure identically.
productionConsiderations.reliability: Always wrap with `%w` as errors cross package boundaries so the top-level handler can make correct decisions and logs retain full context.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Map sentinel and typed errors to circuit-breaker and retry policies; distinguish transient (timeout) from permanent (validation) failures.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Emit structured fields (error type, wrapped chain, request ID) so dashboards can group by error class and alert on spikes.
productionConsiderations.security: Never leak internal wrapped detail to end users; translate errors to safe, generic messages at the boundary while logging the full chain internally.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Avoid retry storms by detecting permanent errors with errors.Is/As and failing fast instead of burning compute on doomed retries.
productionConsiderations.performance: Keep error construction off the hot success path; allocating wrapped errors with stack-trace libraries on every call can dominate CPU under load.

codeExamples.title: Returning and checking errors with errors.New and fmt.Errorf
codeExamples.overview: The foundational (result, error) convention: produce errors two ways and handle them at the call site.
codeExamples.breakdown: divide demonstrates the canonical (T, error) signature: on failure it returns a zero value plus a non-nil error, on success it returns the value plus nil. errors.New is for static messages; fmt.Errorf builds messages with formatting verbs. The caller always checks `if err != nil` before using the result, because the result is meaningless when an error is present.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
10 / 2 = 5
error: division by zero
error: parseAge "-3": negative value -3
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using the result without checking err; ignoring the error with `_`; or calling errors.New with a dynamic string where fmt.Errorf is clearer.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Keep messages lowercase and without trailing punctuation (Go convention) so they compose cleanly when wrapped, e.g. 'open file: ' + underlying message.

codeExamples.title: Wrapping with %w, plus errors.Is and errors.As on a custom type
codeExamples.overview: Build an error chain, then match a sentinel with errors.Is and extract a structured custom error with errors.As.
codeExamples.breakdown: ErrNotFound is a sentinel matched by identity; ValidationError is a struct implementing Error(). service wraps the underlying error with %w so the original stays inspectable. errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) returns true despite the wrapping because it unwraps the chain. errors.As(err, &ve) finds the *ValidationError link and assigns it, giving access to ve.Field. This is exactly how an HTTP handler maps internal errors to status codes.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
chain: service.lookup(id=42): record not found
-> handled as NOT FOUND (404)
chain: service.lookup(id=0): validation: field "id" must be non-zero
-> handled as BAD REQUEST (400), field=id
codeExamples.commonIssues: Using `err == ErrNotFound` (fails after wrapping); passing the value instead of a pointer to errors.As; or wrapping with %v instead of %w, which breaks Is/As.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Only wrap with %w when upstream callers truly need to detect the inner error; otherwise %v keeps the inner error a private implementation detail.

codeExamples.title: The typed-nil-in-interface footgun
codeExamples.overview: Show why returning a nil concrete pointer as an error makes err != nil, and how to fix it.
codeExamples.breakdown: An interface value is non-nil whenever its type descriptor is set, even if the underlying pointer is nil. doBad returns a variable of concrete type *MyError; assigning it to the error interface stamps the type, so `err != nil` is true despite e being nil. doGood avoids the trap by returning the literal nil on success, producing a genuinely nil interface. The rule: never declare a concrete error pointer and return it; return nil explicitly, or return the error interface value directly.
codeExamples.expectedOutput:
doBad reports error: <nil> (type *main.MyError)
doGood: no error
codeExamples.commonIssues: Returning a struct's `err` field typed as *MyError; helper functions that return concrete pointer types later assigned to error; this bug often hides until a 'success' is misreported as failure.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Make functions return the `error` interface type (not *MyError) and always `return nil` on success; lint with `go vet` and tools like nilness/staticcheck which flag this pattern.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: An order-processing API must load a user, charge a payment, and return clear, correctly classified errors so the frontend shows 404 for unknown users, 400 for invalid input, and 503 for transient payment outages while logging full diagnostic context.
endToEndExample.inputData: An HTTP request with a userID and an order amount; downstream a user store (may return a not-found sentinel) and a payment gateway (may return a transient or a permanent custom error).
endToEndExample.architecture: Layered: handler -> service -> repository/gateway. Lower layers return sentinels (ErrUserNotFound) and custom types (*PaymentError with Transient flag). Each layer wraps with fmt.Errorf %w. The handler inspects the final chain with errors.Is / errors.As to choose an HTTP status.
processingSteps: Repository.GetUser returns ErrUserNotFound (sentinel) when the ID is unknown.
Service wraps it: fmt.Errorf("processOrder: %w", err), preserving the sentinel in the chain.
Gateway.Charge returns &PaymentError{Transient: true} on a timeout or {Transient: false} on a declined card.
Service validates the amount up front and returns a *ValidationError for non-positive amounts.
Handler calls errors.Is(err, ErrUserNotFound) -> 404; errors.As for *ValidationError -> 400; errors.As for *PaymentError checks Transient -> 503 or 402.
endToEndExample.output: A correct HTTP status plus a safe client message ('user not found', 'invalid amount', 'payment temporarily unavailable'), while the full wrapped chain is logged internally.
endToEndExample.monitoring: Each error is logged with structured fields: error_class (derived from Is/As), wrapped_message (%v of the chain), user_id, and request_id, enabling per-class alerting on dashboards.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Transient payment errors are retried with backoff before surfacing 503; permanent errors fail fast; unknown errors fall through to a generic 500 with full internal logging but a generic client message.
endToEndExample.finalResult: Clients receive accurate, actionable status codes; operators see grouped, contextual error logs; transient blips self-heal via retry, and the same error value flows cleanly from the lowest layer to the boundary without losing its identity.

industryUseCases.problem: Callers must distinguish a declined card (do not retry) from a network timeout (safe to retry) without parsing message strings.
industryUseCases.solution: Return custom error types implementing error with a category field (e.g. CardError vs APIConnectionError) and let SDKs use errors.As to branch on type.
industryUseCases.benefits: Eliminates fragile string matching, prevents accidental double-charges, and enables correct idempotent retries.

industryUseCases.problem: Controllers must detect 'already exists' or 'not found' API conditions across many wrapped layers of client and reconcile logic.
industryUseCases.solution: The apimachinery package exposes sentinel-like helpers (apierrors.IsNotFound) backed by typed errors, matched after the error propagates through wrapping with %w.
industryUseCases.benefits: Reconcilers make correct create-vs-update decisions and avoid crash loops on expected conditions.

industryUseCases.problem: A query that returns no rows is a normal outcome, not a crash; it must be distinguished from connection failures.
industryUseCases.solution: Compare the query error with errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) to return a 404, while other errors map to 500.
industryUseCases.benefits: Clean separation of 'empty result' from 'broken database', preventing false alerts and correct user-facing responses.

industryUseCases.problem: Users need readable, layered error messages explaining what failed and why, with non-zero exit codes for scripting.
industryUseCases.solution: Wrap errors with fmt.Errorf %w at each step so the top-level main prints the full annotated chain and exits with a meaningful code.
industryUseCases.benefits: Better developer experience, scriptable exit statuses, and easier support triage from copy-pasted error output.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Classify errors into retryable, client-fault, and fatal at well-defined boundaries; under high load this lets the system shed permanent failures immediately rather than queuing doomed work, keeping throughput predictable.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Drive retry, timeout, and circuit-breaker policies off typed errors. Use errors.As to read a Transient or RetryAfter field, and errors.Is to detect known terminal sentinels so the breaker opens only on the right signals.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Map error classes to graceful degradation: a transient dependency error returns a cached or partial response (and 503) rather than cascading a full outage; the wrapped chain is preserved for post-incident analysis.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Persist enough error context (request ID plus full %v chain) in durable logs so that after a regional failover, replayed or stuck operations can be diagnosed and safely re-driven.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Avoid constructing rich, stack-capturing errors on hot success paths; allocate wrapping only when an error actually occurs. Prefer sentinel comparison (cheap) over reflection-heavy patterns in inner loops.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: Detecting permanent errors early with errors.Is/As prevents retry storms that multiply downstream cost; failing fast on validation errors avoids paying for expensive downstream calls that are guaranteed to fail.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: Translate internal errors to safe generic messages at the API boundary so wrapped detail (table names, file paths, internal IPs) never leaks to clients; log the full chain only to internal sinks.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Emit structured logs with a derived error_class field (from Is/As), the wrapped message, and trace IDs; build dashboards that group by class and alert on rate-of-change per class rather than raw counts.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Use custom validation error types (and errors.Join to aggregate many field errors) so a single request reports all validation problems at once, improving data quality and client UX.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Log the error once at the boundary with %+v-style context, not at every layer (which causes duplicate noisy logs); alert on spikes in fatal/unknown classes while treating expected sentinels as informational.

recommendedPractices: Always check `if err != nil` immediately and handle or return before using the result.
Wrap with fmt.Errorf and %w as errors cross package boundaries to add context while keeping the chain inspectable.
Use errors.Is for sentinel comparison and errors.As for type extraction instead of `==` or type assertions on the bare error.
Return the `error` interface type from functions and always `return nil` on success to avoid the typed-nil pitfall.
engineeringStandards: Reserve panic/recover for unrecoverable programmer bugs; never use them as a general control-flow mechanism.
Handle each error exactly once — either wrap-and-return or log-and-handle, never both at every layer.
Keep error messages lowercase and without trailing punctuation so they compose when wrapped.
Run go vet and staticcheck in CI to catch unchecked errors and typed-nil returns.
designRecommendations: Expose sentinels and error types as part of your package's public API only when callers genuinely need to branch on them.
Add context that the caller does not already know (the operation, key inputs) rather than restating the inner message.
Prefer custom error types when you need structured data (codes, fields); prefer sentinels for simple known conditions.
Aggregate independent failures (e.g. multi-field validation) with errors.Join rather than failing on the first.
namingConventions: Name sentinel error variables with an Err prefix: ErrNotFound, ErrTimeout, ErrInvalidInput.
Name custom error types with an Error suffix: ValidationError, PaymentError, ParseError.
Use the receiver convention (e *XxxError) Error() string with a pointer receiver for mutable/structured errors.
Keep wrapping prefixes verb-first and concise: 'load config: %w', 'query users: %w'.
documentationStandards: Document which sentinel errors and error types a function may return so callers know what to inspect.
State whether returned errors are wrapped (and thus Is/As-matchable) in the function's doc comment.
Document the meaning and stability guarantees of any exported ErrXxx (changing its identity is a breaking change).
Show example error-handling code in package docs for the common Is/As branches.
testingStrategies: Assert on errors with errors.Is and errors.As in tests rather than comparing message strings.
Test both the happy path (err == nil) and each distinct failure path explicitly.
Use table-driven tests mapping inputs to expected sentinel/type outcomes.
Add a regression test for the typed-nil case to ensure success returns a genuinely nil error.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring the returned error (assigning to `_` or not checking it).
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: The happy path is tempting and the compiler does not force you to inspect a returned error value.
commonMistakes.impact: Silent failures and corrupted state; bugs surface far from their cause and are hard to trace.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Always check `if err != nil`; if truly unavoidable to handle, document why and at minimum log it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Comparing wrapped errors with `==` instead of errors.Is.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers learn `err == io.EOF` before wrapping exists, and habits persist.
commonMistakes.impact: Once any layer wraps with %w, the `==` check silently stops matching and special-case logic is skipped.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use errors.Is(err, target) for sentinels and errors.As(err, &target) for types, both of which unwrap the chain.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using %v instead of %w when the caller needs to detect the inner error.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: %v and %w produce identical-looking output, so the difference is invisible until inspection fails.
commonMistakes.impact: The underlying error is flattened to a string, so errors.Is/As cannot find it and decisions like retry/404 break.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use %w to wrap when the inner error is part of the contract; reserve %v for when it must stay private.

commonMistakes.mistake: Returning a typed-nil concrete pointer as an error.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: It feels natural to declare `var err *MyError` and return it on both success and failure paths.
commonMistakes.impact: On success the error interface is non-nil, so callers think an operation failed when it succeeded.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Have functions return the `error` interface type and explicitly `return nil` on the success path.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using panic/recover for ordinary, recoverable errors.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers coming from exception-based languages reach for familiar try/catch semantics.
commonMistakes.impact: Non-idiomatic, fragile control flow that can crash the process and is hard to test and reason about.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Return errors for expected failures; reserve panic for unrecoverable programmer bugs and recover only at boundaries.

comparisonSection.explanation: Go returns errors as explicit values checked at the call site; exceptions propagate implicitly up the stack until caught, hiding control flow but reducing boilerplate.
Is/As walk the wrapped chain and are refactor-safe; == and bare type assertions match only the top-level error and break once wrapping is introduced.
%w preserves the inner error so it stays inspectable; %v flattens it to text, hiding it from Is/As — choose based on whether callers must detect the inner error.
Sentinels are simplest for a single known condition matched by identity; custom types carry structured fields and are matched by type, at the cost of more code.
Return errors for expected, handleable failures; use panic only for bugs/impossible states, recovering at boundaries to avoid crashing the whole process.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the error type in Go?
beginnerQuestions.answer: It is a built-in interface with one method: `type error interface { Error() string }`. Any value whose type implements Error() string is an error.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This is the basis of 'errors are values' — there is no special exception class, just an interface, which is why errors can be returned, compared, and wrapped.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you create a basic error and what is the standard return convention?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Use errors.New("message") for a static message or fmt.Errorf("...", args) for a formatted one, and return it as the last value in a (result, error) signature. Callers check `if err != nil`.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Returning error last and nil on success is the universal Go idiom; the result is only valid when err is nil.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between errors.Is and errors.As?
intermediateQuestions.answer: errors.Is reports whether any error in the chain equals (or matches via an Is method) a target sentinel value; errors.As finds the first error in the chain assignable to a target concrete type and assigns it into a pointer you provide.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Is is for identity/sentinel matching (io.EOF, sql.ErrNoRows); As is for recovering structured data from a custom error type. Both unwrap the chain, unlike == or a plain type assertion.

intermediateQuestions.question: What does the %w verb do and how is it different from %v?
intermediateQuestions.answer: %w in fmt.Errorf wraps the given error, producing an error whose Unwrap() returns it, so errors.Is/As can still find it. %v just formats the error as text without preserving it for unwrapping.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Wrapping (%w) maintains an inspectable chain; annotating (%v) flattens to a string. You wrap when the inner error is part of your API contract.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain the typed-nil-in-interface pitfall with errors.
advancedQuestions.answer: An interface value is non-nil whenever its type descriptor is set, regardless of the data pointer. If a function declares `var e *MyError` and returns it (as error) even when e is nil, the returned interface has type *MyError and a nil pointer, so `err != nil` is true.
advancedQuestions.explanation: The fix is to return the `error` interface type and explicitly `return nil` on success, never a concrete typed-nil pointer. This is a frequent source of 'success reported as failure' bugs.

advancedQuestions.question: When should you wrap an error versus annotate it, and when should you not wrap at all?
advancedQuestions.answer: Wrap with %w when upstream callers may legitimately need to detect the underlying error with Is/As. Annotate with %v when the inner error is an implementation detail you do not want to expose. Avoid wrapping when it adds no new context or would leak internal detail across an API boundary.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Wrapping is part of your package's public contract — exposing an inner error means committing to it. Thoughtful wrapping balances debuggability against coupling and security.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: A service that worked yesterday now returns a 500 for a code path that used to special-case 'not found' as a 404, after a refactor added an intermediate layer.
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: A 'used to work' regression after adding a layer that returns errors points at error matching. The new layer likely wraps the error (or the old code used == which no longer matches). Check how the not-found condition is detected at the boundary.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: The handler probably used `err == sql.ErrNoRows` (or the sentinel), which stops matching once the new layer wraps with %w. Replace it with errors.Is(err, sql.ErrNoRows) so it unwraps the chain, and confirm every layer wraps with %w rather than flattening with %v.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an error-handling strategy for a multi-service Go API so that clients get correct HTTP status codes and operators get useful logs.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Lower layers return sentinels and custom typed errors carrying classification fields. Each layer wraps with fmt.Errorf %w to add context. A single middleware/boundary inspects the chain with errors.Is/As, maps to status codes, logs the full chain once with structured fields, and returns a safe generic message to the client.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Wrapping everywhere preserves context but couples callers to inner errors and adds allocation; logging at every layer is noisy, so log once at the boundary. Exposing sentinels is a public-API commitment.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Derive an error_class for metrics and alerting; drive retry/circuit-breaker policy off Transient-style typed fields so the system fails fast on permanent errors and self-heals on transient ones, keeping cost and throughput stable under load.

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: In Go, errors are values implementing `interface { Error() string }`, returned as the last result and checked with `if err != nil`, wrapped with fmt.Errorf %w, and inspected with errors.Is/As.
keyConcepts: error is a one-method interface: Error() string.
Convention: return (result, error); error is last; nil means success.
Wrap context with fmt.Errorf("...: %w", err); peel with errors.Unwrap.
Match sentinels with errors.Is; extract types with errors.As.
Typed nil in an interface is NOT nil — return the error interface and `return nil`.
formulas: extract type: var e *MyError; if errors.As(err, &e) { ... }
commands: go run main.go   # run an example
go vet ./...     # flags unchecked/suspicious error use
staticcheck ./... # deeper lint incl. typed-nil and Is/As misuse
go test ./...    # run error-path tests with errors.Is/As assertions
interviewPoints: Errors are values; Go has no exceptions for normal failures.
panic is for unrecoverable bugs, not ordinary errors.
quickNotes: Sentinels named ErrXxx; custom error types named XxxError.
Lowercase, unpunctuated messages so they compose when wrapped.
Handle an error once: wrap-and-return OR log-and-handle.
Translate to safe messages at the boundary; log full chain internally.
Use errors.As with a pointer to the target variable, e.g. &e.

keyTakeaways: The error interface is a single method, Error() string; treating errors as ordinary values is the heart of Go's explicit, exception-free error model.
Follow the (result, error) convention and the `if err != nil { return err }` idiom; create errors with errors.New / fmt.Errorf and add context by wrapping with %w.
Inspect error chains with errors.Is (sentinels like io.EOF and sql.ErrNoRows) and errors.As (custom XxxError types), never with == or bare type assertions once wrapping is involved.
Beware the typed-nil pitfall: a nil concrete pointer stored in the error interface is non-nil, so return the error interface type and explicitly return nil on success.
Reserve panic/recover for unrecoverable bugs; wrap thoughtfully, log once at the boundary, translate to safe client messages, and classify errors to drive retries and alerting.
